topic.title: What if the Sahara turned green again?

title: The Sahara used to be green. Why?
description:
What happens if the world's biggest hot desert becomes grassland and lakes?
It has happened before, again and again. Here is how, and who would feel it.
Sources: University of Helsinki (Sep 2023).
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.
cta: Green Sahara or melted Antarctica: which what-if should we map next? Comment

lines.text: The Sahara used to be green grassland. So could it really turn green again?
The biggest hot desert on Earth already has, more than 230 times in the last eight million years, flipping from desert to green and back again.
So what flips it? Earth wobbles slowly on its axis, and when the wobble tilts more summer sun onto North Africa, the monsoon rains push north, deep into the sand.
Last time, grass covered the dunes and lakes filled the basins. Hippos, crocodiles and giraffes lived right where camels walk across the sand today.
People herded cattle across it, and painted them on rocks still standing in the Algerian desert today.
But here's the catch. Every year the wind carries Sahara dust across the Atlantic Ocean, thousands of kilometres, all the way to the Amazon rainforest, and that dust feeds its soil.
Turn the Sahara green, and much of that dust stays put on the ground. The world's biggest rainforest, half a world away, would lose one of its fertilisers.
And here's the twist: the wobble comes round about every 21,000 years, so scientists expect the rains to return one day, thousands of years from now.
Green Sahara or melted Antarctica: which what-if should we map next? Tell me in the comments below. And now picture it one more time:

payoff: 'this what-if is not a maybe ... one day ... the green comes back on its own' states a future climate outcome as certain. The script's own source (University of Helsinki, Armstrong et al. 2023; its author's Conversation piece, Dec 2023) says the green periods did not happen during ice ages (high-latitude ice sheets suppressed them), so the 21,000-year wobble does not guarantee a green Sahara every cycle, and today's human-driven warming is a further unknown. Reword as what scientists expect, e.g. 'the wobble comes round about every 21,000 years, so scientists expect the rains to return one day, thousands of years from now', and drop 'not a maybe' and 'on its own'.

(minor, no change needed if kept) fact1 (more than 230 greenings in 8 million years) is not on the cited Helsinki news page; it is confirmed by Larrasoana, Roberts and Rohling, PLoS ONE 2013 (PMC3797788: 'over 230 GSPs within the last 8 million years') and by the Helsinki researcher Edward Armstrong in The Conversation (15 Dec 2023). Consider pointing fact1's url at the PLoS ONE paper or the Conversation article.
